Diabetic ketoacidosis is the one to remember. Either the body adds acid (ketoacids, lactic acid) or it loses the base that normally neutralizes acid, and in both cases bicarbonate falls and the pH drops.

cards.t: Metabolic alkalosis: findings and causes
q: what causes metabolic alkalosis
why does vomiting cause alkalosis
what are the lab findings in metabolic alkalosis
cards.x:
Metabolic alkalosis means a pH above 7.45 with increased bicarbonate. The carbon dioxide is initially normal, and compensation then raises it.

The causes are the mirror image of metabolic acidosis.
- Base gain: excessive bicarbonate administration.
- Acid loss: vomiting, and loss of gastric acids through nasogastric tube suction.
- Potassium depletion and chloride depletion.

Vomiting and suction remove gastric acid, which leaves the blood relatively too basic.

cards.t: Mixed acid-base disorders
k: mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
q: what is a mixed acid-base disorder
which conditions cause mixed disorders
how can heart failure cause both respiratory and metabolic changes
cards.x:
A mixed disorder is more than one acid-base problem at the same time, instead of one primary problem with compensation.

Salicylates and sepsis may both cause a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis.

Congestive heart failure shows how the picture can change over time. Mild failure leads to pulmonary edema and fast breathing, which pushes toward respiratory alkalosis. Severe failure results in hypoperfusion, then lactic acidosis, then metabolic acidosis.

cards.t: Acid-base disorders and potassium shifts
q: how does pH change potassium
why does acidosis cause hyperkalemia
what happens to potassium in alkalosis
cards.x:
Changes in pH cause changes in serum potassium, because potassium moves between the cells and the fluid outside them.

- In acidosis, potassium shifts into the extracellular space, so the blood level rises: hyperkalemia.
- In alkalosis, potassium shifts into the intracellular space, so the blood level falls: hypokalemia.

So the pH and the potassium move in opposite directions, and an abnormal potassium can follow from the pH change.

cards.t: The anion gap: what it is and the formula
q: what is the anion gap
what is the formula for the anion gap
does the anion gap include potassium
cards.x:
The anion gap is the concentration of anions other than chloride and bicarbonate. Serum albumin accounts for most of the normal anion gap. Lactate, ketones, phosphate, sulfate and other organic anions also contribute.

The formula is: anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate). The normal anion gap is 9 to 15, though as with any normal it varies with the source, so a range is given when a gap must be interpreted.

One trap: potassium is not in the formula.

cards.t: How to calculate the anion gap (worked example)
q: how do I calculate the anion gap
what are common anion gap mistakes
can you show a worked anion gap example
cards.x:
Add the chloride and the bicarbonate first, then subtract that total from the sodium.

Worked example, all in mEq/L: sodium 141, chloride 103, bicarbonate 25. Chloride plus bicarbonate is 128. Then 141 minus 128 is a gap of 13, which is inside the normal range of 9 to 15.

The usual slips are to forget the bicarbonate (141 minus 103 gives 38), to add the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it, or to bring in the potassium. Remember the bicarbonate goes in with the chloride, inside the brackets, and the potassium stays out.

cards.t: Elevated anion gap and what it means
q: what causes an elevated anion gap
why is the anion gap high in diabetic ketoacidosis
what are unmeasured anions
cards.x:
An elevated anion gap means the ions the formula leaves out have shifted. Two things can produce it.

- An increase in unmeasured anions: for example anionic proteins (albumin), ketoacids, phosphate and lactate.
- A decrease in unmeasured cations: for example calcium, magnesium, potassium and gamma-globulins.

In diabetic ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis, the elevated gap reflects the extra unmeasured anions, the ketoacids and the lactate. Those anions are not counted in the formula, so they show up as a wider gap.

cards.t: Decreased anion gap and what it means
q: what causes a low anion gap
why does low albumin change the anion gap
what does lithium do to the anion gap
cards.x:
A decreased anion gap points to a short list of causes.

- An increase in unmeasured cations: for example lithium.
- Hypoalbuminemia, meaning low albumin. The gap must be corrected if albumin levels are abnormal.
- Severe hyperlipidemia, which affects the estimates of sodium and chloride.

So a low gap sends you to the albumin, to lithium, or to a lipid problem with the sodium and chloride measurements. A low albumin hides part of the gap, which is why the correction is needed.

cards.t: Correcting the anion gap for albumin
q: how do I correct the anion gap for albumin
why does low albumin hide an elevated anion gap
how much do I add for each drop in albumin
cards.x:
A low albumin hides part of the gap, so the measured gap looks smaller than it really is and you correct it upward.

The rule: add 2.5 mmol/L to the gap for each 1 g/dL of serum albumin below 4.5 g/dL. The correction moves the gap up.

For example, an albumin 1 g/dL below 4.5 means adding 2.5 to the calculated gap, and one 2 g/dL below means adding 5. Use the corrected number when deciding whether the gap is truly elevated.

cards.t: Point-of-care ultrasound versus comprehensive ultrasound
q: what is point-of-care ultrasound
how is POCUS different from a regular ultrasound
who does and reads point-of-care ultrasound
cards.x:
Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a quick, focused scan done at the bedside to give real-time answers to diagnostic questions. The provider who runs the probe also interprets the images. It can be an extension of the history and physical examination, often when the patient may not be able to give enough information.

A comprehensive ultrasound is the full study. It is ordered after the patient has been evaluated, performed by a certified sonographer and interpreted by a radiologist. It is comprehensive, but it takes time: hours to days.

Because the bedside scan is limited and goal directed, it may often still need formal imaging to follow. It is a complement to the rest of the workup, not a replacement.

cards.t: What point-of-care ultrasound is used for
k: what can you scan with POCUS
q: what are the indications for point-of-care ultrasound
what body areas can you scan at the bedside
what are common point-of-care ultrasound applications
cards.x:
Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) covers a wide list of questions. The areas it is used on include trauma, cardiac, pulmonary, vasculature, ophthalmic (eye), renal (kidney), gallbladder, appendix, scrotal and obstetric/gynecologic scanning. The common applications are cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, soft tissue and vascular scanning.

It also comes packaged as protocol-based scans, where several views are combined for one scenario: the extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma (EFAST), the rapid ultrasound in shock and hypotension (RUSH) and the bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE).

And it guides procedures: central venous catheter insertion, paracentesis and thoracentesis. Vascular uses include central lines, ultrasound-guided intravenous lines and deep vein thrombosis scans.

cards.t: Contraindications and limits of point-of-care ultrasound
q: when is point-of-care ultrasound contraindicated
why avoid ultrasound with a globe rupture
what are the limits of bedside ultrasound
cards.x:
Point-of-care ultrasound comes with a few cautions.

- Globe rupture (a ruptured eyeball) is listed as a contraindication for scanning the eye.
- It should not delay lifesaving measures. The scan is for speeding decisions, so it does not come before treatment that cannot wait.
- Some anatomical locations are not amenable to ultrasound, meaning the structure cannot be examined well this way.

So the bedside scan is a helpful extension of the physical examination, not a tool for every question or every patient.

cards.t: Telling an artery from a vein on ultrasound
q: how do you tell an artery from a vein on ultrasound
which vessel compresses completely
why does compressibility matter for vascular procedures
cards.x:
The probe can help tell an artery from a vein by pressing on the vessel. In general, arteries are pulsatile if compressed and have minimal compressibility. Veins are completely compressible, unless they are filled with clot.

That difference identifies structures, especially for vascular procedures such as placing a central line or an ultrasound-guided intravenous line, where you need to be sure which vessel you are looking at.

The clot exception is the useful one: a vein that will not compress is a vein filled with clot.

cards.t: Normal versus abnormal ultrasound findings at a glance
q: what are the abnormal findings on point-of-care ultrasound
what does a normal lung look like on ultrasound
what does an abnormal ultrasound look like for each organ
cards.x:
Each body area has a normal picture and one or two abnormal findings that stand out.

- Lung surface: normal shows A lines (horizontal repeats of the pleural line) and lung sliding. B lines (vertical) mean pulmonary edema. A barcode on M-mode (the motion-mode view) is pneumothorax, and a lung point rules in pneumothorax.
- Gallbladder: normally thin-walled and anechoic (black). A stone with a shadow behind it, wall thickening and fluid around the gallbladder, plus a sonographic Murphy sign, are signs of cholecystitis.
- Veins: normally completely compressible. A vein that will not compress means thrombus.
- Soft tissue: normally orderly layers. Cellulitis gives distortion and cobblestoning; an abscess is an anechoic or hypoechoic collection.
- Inferior vena cava: collapse of more than 50% with inspiration means dehydration or fluid responsiveness.

cards.t: Free fluid in Morison's pouch and the pelvis
q: what is Morison's pouch
how do you see free fluid on ultrasound
what does a dark stripe between the liver and kidney mean
cards.x:
Morison's pouch is the space between the liver and the kidney, and it is one of the places a bedside scan looks for free fluid. Normally the organs sit directly against each other, with no dark stripe between them.

Fluid is anechoic, meaning it returns no echo, so it shows up black. A dark stripe between the gray liver and the kidney is therefore free fluid.

The same idea applies at the spleen and in the pelvis: organs lying against each other with no dark gap is normal, and a dark stripe there is free fluid.

cards.t: How an ultrasound probe makes an image
q: what is ultrasound
how does the probe make an image
what do piezoelectric crystals do
cards.x:
Ultrasound is sound above what human ears can hear, more than 20,000 hertz, used to create an image.

The probe holds tiny piezoelectric crystals. A current makes them vibrate and send out a sound wave. When the echo comes back it vibrates the crystals again, and that vibration is converted back into electricity. The computer turns that signal into a real-time image.

So the same crystals both send the sound and listen for the echo. The image you see is built from how much sound each tissue sends back.

cards.t: Frequency: resolution versus depth
q: what does frequency do in ultrasound
why does a high frequency probe see less deep
how are wavelength and frequency related
cards.x:
Frequency is how often sound waves are emitted, and it trades picture detail against how deep you can see.

- Higher frequency gives better resolution but less depth.
- Lower frequency gives better depth but less resolution.

Wavelength runs the opposite way: a short wavelength means a high frequency, and a long wavelength means a low frequency.

So when you want finer detail, you choose a higher frequency and accept less depth. When you need to see deeper, you choose a lower frequency and accept less detail.

cards.t: Gain and depth on the machine
q: what does gain do on ultrasound
what is depth on an ultrasound machine
what is the difference between gain and depth
cards.x:
Two controls you will adjust constantly are depth and gain.

Depth is how far you are zoomed in. Gain is brightness: turning it up makes the picture brighter and turning it down makes it darker.

They are easy to mix up because both change how the image looks, but they do different jobs: depth is about zoom, and gain is only about brightness.

cards.t: Probe types and probe movements
k: fan rock sweep slide rotate compress
q: what types of ultrasound probes are there
what are the probe movements
why choose a different transducer
cards.x:
Different probes suit different sites. The four to know are the phased array, linear, curvilinear and endocavitary probes. Choosing the right transducer for the body area is part of getting a good image.

There are also six named ways to move the probe: fanning, rocking, sweeping, sliding, rotating and compressing.

The probe types and these movements together are what the term knobology covers.

cards.t: The probe indicator and scan planes
q: what is the indicator on an ultrasound probe
which way should the probe marker point
what are the ultrasound planes
cards.x:
Every probe has an indicator, also called the probe marker or orientation marker, on one side. It orients you to the image: the dot on the screen matches the side of the probe that carries the marker.

Keep the indicator pointed to your left, which is the patient's right. Cardiology puts it the opposite way. The marker should always match the orientation marker on the screen.

The three planes are:
- Transverse (axial): indicator to your left, looking through the patient.
- Sagittal (longitudinal).
- Coronal (frontal).

cards.t: Echogenicity: anechoic, hypoechoic, hyperechoic, isoechoic
q: what does anechoic mean
what is the difference between hypoechoic and hyperechoic
what does isoechoic mean
cards.x:
Echogenicity is how bright a tissue looks compared with another tissue. The more echo it sends back, the brighter it is.

- Anechoic: black. It returns no echo, as with fluid-filled structures.
- Hypoechoic: gray. It returns less echo than its surroundings, as the liver and spleen do.
- Hyperechoic: white. It is dense and returns more echo than its surroundings, as bone and stones do.
- Isoechoic: the same brightness as its surroundings, because it has the same density.

Helpful memory: hypo means less echo and hyper means more echo.

cards.t: Acoustic shadowing
k: dark band behind ribs or stones
q: what is acoustic shadowing
why is there a dark band behind a rib or a stone
what causes a posterior acoustic shadow
cards.x:
Acoustic shadowing happens with hyperechoic structures, and it shows up as a dark band behind them. Ribs and stones are the classic examples: you see a bright rib or gallstone with a dark band behind it.

Air can shadow too, but it looks dirtier than the shadow from bone.

It is a useful clue. A bright stone in the gallbladder with a shadow behind it is the picture of a stone with a posterior acoustic shadow, one of the findings of cholecystitis.

cards.t: Posterior acoustic enhancement
q: what is posterior acoustic enhancement
why is it bright behind a full bladder
how is enhancement different from shadowing
cards.x:
Posterior acoustic enhancement is the opposite of shadowing. When sound passes through a fluid-filled structure, the images deep to it come out bright. A bright area behind the bladder or the gallbladder is the usual example.

The brightness can be a problem as well as a clue, because it can obscure the structures sitting behind the fluid.

Quick way to separate the two: a dark band behind a structure is shadowing, which goes with dense, hyperechoic objects like ribs and stones. A bright area behind a structure is enhancement, which goes with fluid.

cards.t: Edge artifact
q: what is edge artifact
what causes a dark line off the edge of the gallbladder or bladder
is edge artifact a refraction or reverberation artifact
cards.x:
Edge artifact is a refraction artifact. Refraction means the sound waves bend. When they meet the curved edge of a fluid-filled structure they bend off it, and the result is a dark line running off the edge of the structure.

So the thing to recognize is a dark line coming off the curved edge of a fluid-filled structure.

Do not mix it up with the mirror image artifact, which is a reverberation artifact, or with acoustic shadowing, which is a dark band behind a hyperechoic structure.

cards.t: Mirror image artifact
q: what is mirror image artifact
why is the liver seen above the diaphragm
why does a normal lung ultrasound show a mirrored liver
cards.x:
Mirror image artifact is a reverberation artifact. Sound hits a strong reflector and the image is mirrored on the other side of it, like an object and its reflection.

The normal example is the liver copied above the diaphragm. Air is an acoustic barrier, and above the diaphragm the liver is mirrored.

That is why losing the mirror image matters. When the mirroring is absent above the diaphragm, along with the spine sign, that points to a pleural effusion.

cards.t: Ring down and side lobe artifacts
q: what is ring down artifact
what is side lobe artifact
what causes bright streaks from air in the bile ducts
cards.x:
Ring down and side lobe artifacts each have their own cause and example, so tie each to its own.

- Ring down artifact is caused by foci of air. It shows as bright streaks, as with hepatic pneumobilia (air in the bile ducts).
- Side lobe artifact happens when sound reflected by a strong reflector outside the central beam appears as if it is in the beam. The example is echoes inside the gallbladder lumen (its hollow space).

Both are artifacts, so you recognize them by their pattern and example.

cards.t: A lines, B lines and comet tails
q: what are A lines
what are B lines
what are comet tails
how do A lines differ from B lines
cards.x:
All three are reverberation artifacts.

- A lines: horizontal repeats of the pleural line. This is the normal lung.
- B lines: vertical hyperechoic lines in the lung that come from an air-water interface. The example is pulmonary edema.
- Comet tails: vertical hyperechoic lines that may come off calcifications, cholesterol or metal. Short bright tails off the gallbladder wall are the example.

Quick way to tell them apart: A lines run sideways and are normal lung. B lines run up and down in the lung and go with pulmonary edema.

cards.t: B-mode versus M-mode
q: what is B-mode
what is M-mode used for
what is the difference between B-mode and M-mode
cards.x:
B-mode (brightness mode) is the standard view: shades of gray that build a two-dimensional image.

M-mode (motion mode) takes one line of that B-mode image and shows its movement over time. So where B-mode shows a picture, M-mode shows a single line of the picture changing with time.

Common uses are fetal ultrasound (for example, the fetal heart) and pneumothorax.

cards.t: The seashore sign and the barcode sign on M-mode
q: what is the seashore sign
what is the barcode sign
how does M-mode show a pneumothorax
cards.x:
M-mode through the lung gives one of two patterns.

Normal lung is the seashore. Above the pleural line the lines are smooth, like the ocean, and below it the picture is grainy, like sand on the beach. Seeing a seashore means there is no pneumothorax.

Pneumothorax is the barcode. The smooth lines run all the way down with no grainy sand below, so the picture looks like the stripes of a barcode.

Memory aid: a beach means normal, and a barcode means a pneumothorax.

cards.t: Color Doppler and BART
q: what does color Doppler show
what does BART stand for
do red and blue mean arteries and veins
cards.x:
Color Doppler shows the direction and velocity of flow, represented by color. The memory aid is BART (Blue Away, Red Towards). Flow toward the probe is red, flow away from the probe is blue, and flow perpendicular to the beam shows as black.

Blue and red do not necessarily mean venous and arterial, so do not read the colors as vein and artery.

Color Doppler has its own artifacts too, called twinkle artifact and aliasing.

cards.t: The four cardiac windows
q: what are the four cardiac ultrasound windows
which probe is used for cardiac ultrasound
how many views does bedside cardiac ultrasound use
cards.x:
Bedside cardiac scanning uses the phased array (cardiac) probe and four main viewing windows:

- Parasternal long axis
- Parasternal short axis
- Subxiphoid (also called subcostal)
- Apical four chamber

Each window looks at the heart from a different place on the chest or abdomen, and each is best at showing certain things. The parasternal long axis is often the easiest to get, the apical four chamber is sometimes difficult to obtain, and the subxiphoid view uses the liver as its window.

cards.t: Parasternal long axis view
k: long axis view of the heart
q: what is the parasternal long axis view
what do you see in parasternal long axis
which cardiac window is easiest to get
cards.x:
The parasternal long axis view is taken beside the sternum, and it lays the heart out lengthwise. On the screen you see the right ventricle on top, then the left ventricle, the aorta and the left atrium.

It is often the easiest cardiac view to obtain.

Rotate the probe 90 degrees from here and you reach the parasternal short axis view, a cross-section of the ventricles.

cards.t: Parasternal short axis view
k: short axis view of the heart
q: what is the parasternal short axis view
how do you get from long axis to short axis
what does the parasternal short axis show
cards.x:
To get the parasternal short axis view, start from the long axis and rotate the probe 90 degrees so the marker points toward the patient's right hip.

The picture changes from a lengthwise view to a cross-section of the ventricles, like slicing across the heart instead of along it.

This window gives a good view of the mitral and aortic valves.

cards.t: Subxiphoid view and pericardial effusion
q: which cardiac view is best for pericardial effusion
why use the subxiphoid view
where do you put the probe for a subxiphoid view
cards.x:
The subxiphoid (subcostal) view is the best view for a pericardial effusion, which is fluid around the heart. The reason is that most effusions are inferior, meaning they collect toward the bottom of the heart, and this window looks up at the heart from below.

The probe goes under the xiphoid, just to the patient's right of midline. It uses the liver as a window, so on the screen the liver sits on top with the heart beneath it.

So when the question is whether there is fluid around the heart, think subxiphoid first.

cards.t: Apical four chamber and five chamber views
q: what does the apical four chamber view show
why use the apical four chamber view
what is the five chamber view
cards.x:
The apical four chamber view is taken at the apex of the heart and shows all four chambers at once. It is sometimes difficult to obtain.

It is important for right ventricular dilation or strain, because it shows all four chambers at once.

If you rotate the probe, you get the five chamber view, which adds the aortic valve and the outflow tract (the path blood takes out of the left ventricle).

cards.t: Which probe for which lung finding
q: which probe is used for pneumothorax
which probe is used for pleural effusion and pneumonia
what probe do you use for lung ultrasound
cards.x:
The probe choice follows the finding you are looking for.

- Linear probe: pneumothorax.
- Curvilinear probe: pleural effusion, pulmonary edema and pneumonia.

Multiple anterior and posterior views of the chest are available, so one patient can be scanned in several places.

So pair pneumothorax with the linear probe, and effusion, edema and pneumonia with the curvilinear probe. The lung can also be scanned with protocols such as the bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE) protocol.

cards.t: The BLUE protocol
q: what is the BLUE protocol
how does the BLUE protocol sort the cause of shortness of breath
what do the A profile and B profile mean
cards.x:
The bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE) protocol sorts sudden shortness of breath using the lung findings, starting with whether lung sliding is present.

With lung sliding present:
- B-profile: pulmonary edema.
- A-profile: check the veins. A thrombosed vein points to pulmonary embolism. Free veins with PLAPS (posterolateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome) point to pneumonia. Free veins without PLAPS point to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma.
- A/B or C-profile: pneumonia.

With sliding abolished:
- B-prime profile: pneumonia.
- A-prime profile plus a lung point: pneumothorax.

cards.t: Pulmonary edema on ultrasound
q: how does pulmonary edema look on ultrasound
what do B lines mean
which probe shows pulmonary edema
cards.x:
Pulmonary edema shows up as B lines. These are vertical hyperechoic (bright) lines in the lung that come from an air-water interface.

The curvilinear probe is used for it. In the bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE) protocol, a B-profile with lung sliding present points to pulmonary edema.

Contrast: a normal lung shows A lines, which are horizontal repeats of the pleural line, not vertical lines.

cards.t: Pleural effusion and the spine sign
q: how does a pleural effusion look on ultrasound
what is the spine sign
why does an effusion lose the mirror image
cards.x:
A pleural effusion shows as dark fluid above the diaphragm.

Normally air in the lung is an acoustic barrier, so above the diaphragm you see a mirrored copy of the liver. With an effusion, fluid lets sound pass through easily instead of blocking it, so the mirror image is absent and the thoracic vertebrae can be seen through the fluid. That sight of the spine is the spine sign.

So the two clues are dark fluid above the diaphragm, with no mirroring and the spine visible. The curvilinear probe is used.

cards.t: Pneumonia on ultrasound
q: what does pneumonia look like on ultrasound
what is hepatization
what are bronchograms
cards.x:
Aerated lung normally shows only artifacts. In pneumonia you can see:

- Bronchograms: air, fluid or consolidations in the bronchi.
- B lines.
- Hepatization: the lung looks like liver.
- Pleural effusions or empyema.
- The spine sign.

In the bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE) protocol, several profiles lead to pneumonia, including a mixed A/B profile, a C-profile, or a B-prime profile when sliding is abolished. The curvilinear probe is used.

cards.t: Lung sliding, the lung point and pneumothorax
q: what is the lung point
how do you diagnose pneumothorax on ultrasound
what does abolished lung sliding mean
cards.x:
Lung sliding is a normal finding at the surface of the lung, listed alongside A lines and the seashore pattern on M-mode (the motion-mode view). Pneumothorax is different: it shows an M-mode barcode (not the seashore) and a lung point. A lung point rules in pneumothorax.

In the bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE) protocol, sliding abolished (gone) with an A-prime profile plus a lung point leads to pneumothorax. The linear probe is used.

cards.t: Cholecystitis on ultrasound
q: what does cholecystitis look like on ultrasound
what is the sonographic Murphy sign
what findings suggest cholecystitis
cards.x:
A normal gallbladder is thin-walled and anechoic (black inside). Cholecystitis, inflammation of the gallbladder, shows up as a group of findings:

- A stone, with a posterior acoustic shadow (a dark band behind it).
- Wall thickening.
- Pericholecystic fluid, which is fluid around the gallbladder.
- A sonographic Murphy sign.

The stone, thickened wall and surrounding fluid, plus the sonographic Murphy sign, are the signs of cholecystitis. The stone-and-shadow pairing is the same shadowing artifact you see behind ribs.

cards.t: The inferior vena cava and volume status
q: how does the inferior vena cava show volume status
what does more than 50% collapse of the inferior vena cava mean
where do you put the probe to see the inferior vena cava
cards.x:
The inferior vena cava (the large vein returning blood to the heart from the lower body) helps determine volume status, meaning how full the patient is, and fluid responsiveness, meaning whether fluids are likely to help.

The probe is placed longitudinally, just right of midline. Collapse of more than 50% with inspiration indicates dehydration or fluid responsiveness.

This is the scan that answers the volume question in a hypotensive patient.

cards.t: Aorta versus inferior vena cava on ultrasound
q: how do you tell the aorta from the inferior vena cava
which vessel is compressible
how do arteries and veins differ under the probe
cards.x:
The aorta and the inferior vena cava can both be seen in cross-section, above the shadow of the vertebral body.

The way to tell them apart is how they respond to pressure:
- The aorta, like all arteries, is pulsatile with minimal compressibility.
- The inferior vena cava, like all veins, is completely compressible, unless it is filled with clot.

A vein that will not compress is therefore suspicious for thrombus, while an artery is not expected to flatten.

cards.t: Protocols: EFAST, BLUE and RUSH
k: focused assessment with sonography in trauma
rapid ultrasound in shock and hypotension
q: what is the difference between EFAST, BLUE and RUSH
what is the RUSH exam
which ultrasound protocol is for trauma
cards.x:
A protocol combines several views for one scenario. Match each protocol to its scenario:

- FAST (focused assessment with sonography in trauma) and EFAST (the extended version): trauma.
- BLUE (bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency): the lungs.
- RUSH (rapid ultrasound in shock and hypotension): shock or low blood pressure.

So the scenario tells you which protocol to use: trauma, lungs, or shock and low blood pressure.

cards.t: The six EFAST windows
q: what are the EFAST windows
where do you look for pericardial effusion in EFAST
which EFAST views look for pneumothorax
cards.x:
The extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma (EFAST) uses six windows, each answering a question:

1. Right upper quadrant: peritoneal and pleural free fluid.
2. Left upper quadrant: peritoneal and pleural free fluid.
3. Suprapubic: peritoneal free fluid.
4. Subxiphoid or parasternal: pericardial effusion.
5 and 6. Right and left anterior chest: pneumothorax.

So one pass covers free fluid in the abdomen and chest, fluid around the heart, and a collapsed lung.

cards.t: Cellulitis on ultrasound
q: how does cellulitis look on ultrasound
what is cobblestoning
how is cellulitis different from normal soft tissue on ultrasound
cards.x:
Normal soft tissue shows orderly layers on ultrasound. Cellulitis, an infection of the skin and soft tissue beneath it, breaks up that order. The findings are distortion of the soft tissue and cobblestoning, a pattern that looks like the rounded stones of a cobblestone road.

So the scan is looking for a change in the normal layered pattern.

Quick way to tell it from an abscess: cellulitis is a distorted, cobblestoned tissue pattern, while an abscess is an anechoic or hypoechoic collection whose pus shifts when you compress it.

cards.t: Abscess on ultrasound
q: how does an abscess look on ultrasound
what is the compression sign for an abscess
how do you tell an abscess from cellulitis on ultrasound
cards.x:
An abscess appears as an anechoic or hypoechoic collection, meaning dark or gray. How it looks can vary a lot.

The helpful test is to press on it: pus will shift when you compress with the probe.

Quick way to tell it from cellulitis: cellulitis gives distortion and cobblestoning of the tissue layers, while an abscess is a collection whose pus shifts under pressure.

cards.t: Deep vein thrombosis on compression ultrasound
q: how do you diagnose a deep vein thrombosis on ultrasound
what is the main finding of a deep vein thrombosis
why is compressibility the test for a clot
cards.x:
In a deep vein thrombosis (a blood clot in a deep vein), the major diagnostic feature is that the vein is not compressible. A normal vein is completely compressible, so it flattens when you press the probe on it. A vein holding thrombus will not flatten, so the test is the compression.

Depending on chronicity (how old the clot is), the content may be hypoechoic (less echo, gray) or hyperechoic (more echo, white). There may also be loss of color flow.

So the key question to answer is whether the vein flattens. If it will not compress, suspect thrombus.

cards.t: When a bedside scan is not the answer
q: when should I not use point-of-care ultrasound
should a stable patient with a possible DVT get a bedside scan
when does point-of-care ultrasound earn its place
cards.x:
A bedside scan earns its place when the question cannot wait. Take a patient in sudden, undifferentiated respiratory distress: an unstable patient like that needs a bedside answer now, and a quick scan can give one.

Now take a stable patient with leg pain and swelling after a knee replacement, no chest pain or shortness of breath, and normal vital signs. A deep vein thrombosis (a blood clot in a deep vein) is likely, but the patient is stable. The answer for this patient is a formal ultrasound, probably not point-of-care ultrasound. Current practice also accepts a point-of-care compression ultrasound for a suspected deep vein thrombosis in trained hands.

cards.t: Integrating the bedside scan into the decision
k: combining ultrasound with history and exam
q: how does point-of-care ultrasound fit into a clinical decision
when do you need a bedside answer now
how do you combine the scan with the history and vital signs
cards.x:
Point-of-care ultrasound is integrated with the history, the physical examination and the vital signs, not used on its own.

The principle is that an unstable, undifferentiated patient needs a bedside answer now. Sudden respiratory distress with very high blood pressure, then diffuse crackles and dyspnea (shortness of breath) without chest pain, is that kind of patient. The scan, together with the story and the vital signs, points to the cause.

A stable patient is different. Stable leg pain and swelling after a knee replacement, with no chest pain or shortness of breath and normal vital signs, is likely a deep vein thrombosis, and the answer there is formal ultrasound, probably not point-of-care.

cards.t: Flash pulmonary edema with diffuse B lines
k: sudden respiratory distress with high blood pressure
q: how do you recognize flash pulmonary edema at the bedside
what is SCAPE
what findings point to flash pulmonary edema
cards.x:
Flash pulmonary edema is sudden fluid in the lungs. One case shows how the pieces fit: sudden, undifferentiated respiratory distress, very high blood pressure, then diffuse crackles and dyspnea (shortness of breath) without chest pain.

Diffuse B lines on the scan, together with the crackles and the blood pressure, point to flash pulmonary edema. It is also called SCAPE (sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema).

In that case the patient improved on bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) and a nitroglycerin drip.

cards.t: How the protocols build in integration
q: what questions does EFAST answer
how does BLUE sort shortness of breath
how does the inferior vena cava answer the volume question
cards.x:
The protocols are integration built in, so each answers a whole set of questions in one pass.

- The extended focused assessment with sonography in trauma (EFAST) answers the trauma questions: free fluid, pericardial effusion and pneumothorax.
- The inferior vena cava answers the volume question in a hypotensive patient.
- The bilateral lung ultrasound in emergency (BLUE) protocol sorts acute dyspnea (shortness of breath) into edema, embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax and obstructive disease.

Each one takes a broad emergency question and answers it with a set of views combined for one scenario.

cards.t: Why fatal ABO incompatibility is a bedside error
q: why do fatal transfusion reactions happen
what is wrong blood in tube
is a fatal ABO mismatch a lab error
cards.x:
Fatal ABO (blood group system) incompatibility is almost always a clerical mistake, not a laboratory mistake. The blood bank's testing was accurate; the blood simply went to the wrong patient.

Picture a trauma patient in bay 1 who gets a unit meant for bay 2. Within 5 minutes the patient has rigors, severe flank pain, fast breathing, sudden low blood pressure and dark port-wine urine. The root cause is either a mislabeled sample ("wrong blood in tube") or a failure of two-person verification at the bedside.

That gives the first cardinal rule: human error drives mortality. Most fatal hemolytic reactions come from bedside clerical errors, so verify the patient's identity and the blood unit at the bedside.

cards.t: Bedside sample labeling and two-identifier verification
q: how should a blood sample tube be labeled
what identifiers are checked before a transfusion
can you pre-label blood tubes
cards.x:
Two habits stop wrong-blood mistakes.

- Label the sample tube immediately at the bedside, in front of the patient. Never pre-label tubes, and never label them away from the patient.
- Verify with two identifiers: match the patient name, medical record number, the unit's blood type and the unit's serial number directly against the patient's wristband.

Both habits matter because a mislabeled sample or a skipped check at the bedside is how the wrong blood reaches the wrong patient.

cards.t: The critical first 15 minutes of a transfusion
q: why is a transfusion started slowly
how fast do acute hemolytic reactions appear
what happens in the first 15 minutes of a transfusion
cards.x:
The first 15 minutes are the critical window. The first 25 to 50 mL is infused slowly, because severe acute hemolytic reactions show up rapidly, after as little as 25 mL.

A slow start means that if the unit is incompatible, only a small amount has gone in by the time the warning signs appear, and the transfusion can be stopped early.

cards.t: The second-sample rule for blood type
k: no prior blood type on record
q: what is the second sample rule
when do you need a second blood sample
why draw a second type and screen sample
cards.x:
If a patient has no prior verified blood type on record, a second, separate sample must be drawn and tested to confirm the ABO (blood group system) and Rh type.

This guards against the wrong-blood-in-tube problem, since a mislabeled sample is one root cause of fatal ABO incompatibility: a second, separate sample gives an independent confirmation of the first result.

cards.t: ABO antigens: sugars on the red cell surface
q: what are the A and B antigens
why does group O have no A or B antigen
what is the H antigen
cards.x:
The A and B antigens are oligosaccharides, which are short chains of sugars, attached to glycoproteins in the red cell membrane.

- Group O has only the unmodified H antigen core structure, with no A or B sugars.
- Group A possesses an enzyme called N-acetylgalactosamine transferase.
- Group B possesses an enzyme called D-galactosyltransferase.
- Group AB (the group with both antigens) expresses the A and the B antigen at the same time.

These are carbohydrates, which is what separates them from the RhD protein.

cards.t: Naturally occurring antibodies and Landsteiner's rule
q: what is Landsteiner's rule
why do people have anti-A or anti-B without being transfused
why is immunoglobulin M important in ABO
cards.x:
Landsteiner's rule says you always produce antibodies against the ABO (blood group system) antigens that are absent from your own red blood cells. So group A makes anti-B, group B makes anti-A, group O makes both and group AB (both A and B antigens) makes neither.

These antibodies are called naturally occurring because you form them without ever being transfused. They are triggered in infancy, when cross-reactive gut flora and food carbohydrates prime the immune system.

They are mostly immunoglobulin M, a large pentameric (five-part) antibody that is very efficient at fixing complement by binding C1q. That is why an ABO mismatch can turn dangerous so fast.

cards.t: How an ABO mismatch destroys red cells
k: why ABO mismatch causes shock and DIC
q: how does an ABO mismatch cause hemolysis
why does ABO incompatibility cause shock
why does ABO incompatibility cause kidney damage
cards.x:
In an ABO (blood group system) mismatch, the recipient's immunoglobulin M antibodies meet the donor cells' antigens, and the damage happens in the bloodstream itself.

- Complement activation: the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) assembles fully in the circulation.
- Immediate lysis: red cells rupture and release free hemoglobin into the plasma (hemoglobinemia).
- Vasoactive storm: the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a cause widespread vasodilation, low blood pressure and shock.
- Renal and clotting crisis: free hemoglobin precipitates in the kidney tubules and causes acute tubular necrosis, and microvascular procoagulants trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation.

cards.t: Which red cells each blood group can receive
q: who is the universal red cell donor
who can receive which red cells
why can AB receive any red cells
cards.x:
For red cell transfusions, the question is whether the donor cells carry an antigen that the recipient's antibodies will attack.

- Group O (anti-A and anti-B): can receive O only, can give to O, A, B and AB (both antigens). Group O red cells have no ABO (blood group system) antigens to react with, so O is the universal red cell donor.
- Group A (anti-B): receives A or O, gives to A or AB.
- Group B (anti-A): receives B or O, gives to B or AB.
- Group AB (no antibodies): receives AB, A, B or O, gives to AB only. AB is the universal red cell recipient.

cards.t: Plasma compatibility runs opposite to red cells
q: who is the universal plasma donor
why is plasma compatibility the opposite of red cells
who is the universal plasma recipient
cards.x:
Plasma carries antibodies rather than antigens that matter, so the red cell rules run in the opposite direction.

- Red cells: group O is the universal donor and group AB (both A and B antigens) is the universal recipient.
- Plasma: group AB is the universal plasma donor, because its plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B. Group O is the universal plasma recipient.

To keep it straight, ask what is being given. With red cells, the donor's antigens are the risk. With plasma, the donor's antibodies are the risk, and AB plasma has none of the ABO (blood group system) ones.

cards.t: Emergency release: O-negative red cells
q: who gets O-negative blood in an emergency
why give O-negative to young women in trauma
what is emergency release blood
cards.x:
Only about 6 to 7% of the US population is O-negative, so it is kept as a strict emergency reserve. It is mandatory for females of childbearing potential (younger than 50) with an unknown blood type in acute trauma.

The reason is preventing alloimmunization (making antibodies to a foreign antigen). If a young female is accidentally exposed to RhD, she risks lifelong anti-D formation and fetal hydrops (severe fetal swelling from anemia) in future pregnancies.

In an emergency release, the unit is sent uncrossmatched while the blood bank runs rapid confirmatory testing.

cards.t: Emergency release: O-positive red cells in massive hemorrhage
k: Rh negative male given Rh positive blood
q: when can O-positive blood be used in an emergency
what happens if an Rh-negative man gets O-positive blood
why is O-positive used in massive transfusion
cards.x:
About 37 to 39% of the population is O-positive, so O-positive red cells are the standard in the massive transfusion protocol for adult males and post-menopausal females. That saves the scarce O-negative supply for the patients who need it most.

An Rh-negative male given O-positive red cells will not suffer immediate acute intravascular hemolysis, because Rh-negative people have no anti-D at baseline.

There is still a calculated risk: anti-D may form later. But surviving acute hemorrhagic shock takes clinical precedence.

cards.t: The RhD antigen and why exposure is needed first
q: what is the RhD antigen
what does Rh-positive mean
why do Rh-negative people not have anti-D at baseline
cards.x:
RhD is a transmembrane structural protein, unlike the ABO (blood group system) carbohydrates. It is highly immunogenic (good at provoking an immune response), the most immunogenic red cell antigen outside the ABO system.

"Rh-positive" strictly means the RhD polypeptide is present, and "Rh-negative" means it is absent. About 85% of Caucasians and more than 90% of African Americans and Asians are RhD-positive.

The key difference from ABO: Rh-negative people have zero pre-existing anti-D. Sensitization is required first, through transfusion of Rh-positive red cells or feto-maternal hemorrhage (fetal blood entering the mother's circulation) during pregnancy or delivery.

cards.t: Anti-D: an acquired IgG that takes time to form
q: what kind of antibody is anti-D
why does anti-D take weeks to appear
is anti-D the same as the naturally occurring ABO antibodies
cards.x:
Anti-D is a monomeric immunoglobulin G antibody, predominantly the IgG1 and IgG3 subclasses. It is not naturally occurring. It appears only after an Rh-negative person is exposed to RhD.

It also appears slowly. The primary response has to switch from immunoglobulin M to immunoglobulin G, and that takes weeks to months to mature. So a first exposure does not cause an immediate reaction, which is the opposite of the instant ABO (blood group system) picture.

cards.t: How Rh antibodies destroy red cells (extravascular hemolysis)
q: how does anti-D destroy red cells
why is an Rh reaction gradual
does anti-D cause shock
cards.x:
Anti-D coats the red cells, and the spleen cleans them up. Splenic Fc-gamma receptors recognize the immunoglobulin G coating. The opsonized (antibody-tagged) cells are then destroyed by macrophages in the reticuloendothelial system.

Because the cells are removed in the spleen rather than burst in the bloodstream, the course is gradual: spherocyte formation (small round red cells), mild hyperbilirubinemia and low haptoglobin.

This kind of destruction rarely triggers acute complement-mediated intravascular collapse or disseminated intravascular coagulation, so shock is not part of the picture.

cards.t: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn from Rh incompatibility
q: what is hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
why does the second Rh-positive pregnancy get hurt
how does an Rh-negative mother get sensitized
cards.x:
This is what happens when an RhD-negative mother carries an RhD-positive fetus.

- Sensitization: fetal blood crosses into her circulation (transplacental feto-maternal hemorrhage) during delivery or trauma.
- She mounts an immune response and makes high-affinity immunoglobulin G anti-D.
- In later pregnancies, that immunoglobulin G readily crosses the placenta through Fc receptors on the syncytiotrophoblast.
- In the fetus, anti-D binds fetal red cells, and the spleen destroys them. The result is profound anemia, extramedullary hematopoiesis (blood making outside the marrow) and high-output heart failure, called hydrops fetalis.

So the sensitizing event comes first, and the harm to the baby comes in subsequent pregnancies, when her immunoglobulin G crosses the placenta.

cards.t: How Rh immune globulin prevents sensitization
q: how does Rh immune globulin work
what is Rh immune globulin
who gets Rh immune globulin
cards.x:
Rh immune globulin is anti-D given to an RhD-negative mother who is not yet sensitized. The given anti-D binds and masks the fetal D-positive red cells, clearing them before the mother's own B cells can mount an immune response.

So it works by stopping her from becoming sensitized in the first place. It is meant for non-sensitized RhD-negative mothers, who have not yet formed their own anti-D.

cards.t: When Rh immune globulin is given
q: when is Rh immune globulin given in pregnancy
what events need Rh immune globulin
how soon after delivery is Rh immune globulin given
cards.x:
For non-sensitized RhD-negative mothers, Rh immune globulin is given at set times.

- Routine prophylaxis: at about 28 weeks of gestation.
- Post-partum: within 72 hours of delivering an RhD-positive neonate.
- After potentially sensitizing events, when fetal blood could enter the mother's circulation: miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, abortion, amniocentesis or abdominal trauma.

Each time point is an opportunity for fetal red cells to reach the mother, so the antibody is given to clear them before she responds.

cards.t: Kleihauer-Betke test
q: what is the Kleihauer-Betke test
how do you know if more Rh immune globulin is needed
why measure fetal-maternal hemorrhage
cards.x:
The Kleihauer-Betke test measures how much fetal blood has entered the mother's circulation, the volume of fetal-maternal hemorrhage.

It is used to calculate whether additional vials of Rh immune globulin are required. A larger bleed means more fetal red cells to clear, so one vial may not be enough.

cards.t: ABO against RhD, head to head
k: difference between ABO and Rh antibodies
q: what is the difference between ABO and Rh reactions
why is ABO more dangerous than Rh
which is intravascular and which is extravascular
cards.x:
ABO (blood group system) and Rh follow different rules.

- Antigen: ABO antigens are carbohydrate oligosaccharides (A, B, H); RhD is a transmembrane protein.
- Baseline antibodies: ABO antibodies are naturally occurring; Rh antibodies are absent until sensitized by transfusion or pregnancy.
- Antibody class: ABO is immunoglobulin M, a pentamer and avid complement activator; Rh is immunoglobulin G, a monomer that crosses the placenta.
- Hemolysis site: ABO is intravascular (cells lysed in the circulation); Rh is extravascular (splenic reticuloendothelial system).
- Severity: ABO is acute and dramatic, with shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and acute tubular necrosis; Rh is gradual, with a drop in hemoglobin and mild jaundice.

cards.t: ABO typing: forward and reverse must agree
q: what is forward and reverse typing
why must forward and reverse typing match
what is an ABO discrepancy
cards.x:
ABO (blood group system) typing is done two ways, and the two answers must agree.

- Forward typing tests the patient's washed red cells with commercial monoclonal anti-A and anti-B. It is direct agglutination (clumping) and shows which antigens are present.
- Reverse typing tests the patient's plasma or serum against known reagent red cells (A1 cells and B cells). It detects the expected reciprocal antibodies, the isohemagglutinins.

The discrepancy rule: forward and reverse types must match before blood is released. Any discrepancy prompts immediate investigation.

cards.t: Reading forward and reverse typing results
q: how do I read ABO typing results
what does agglutination with anti-A mean
how does the reverse type look for group O and AB
cards.x:
Each result in the forward type is matched by an expected result in the reverse type.

- Agglutination with anti-A means the A antigen is present; in the reverse type only the B cells agglutinate, because anti-B is present. That is group A.
- Agglutination with anti-B means the B antigen is present; only the reagent cells that carry the A antigen agglutinate, because anti-A is present. That is group B.
- No agglutination with anti-A or anti-B is group O in the forward type; in the reverse type both reagent cell types agglutinate.
- If the reverse type shows no agglutination of either reagent cell, the group is AB (both A and B antigens).

Agglutination with anti-D means the patient is Rh(D) positive.

cards.t: Antibody screen (indirect antiglobulin test)
q: what is an antibody screen
what does a positive antibody screen mean
how does an antibody screen work
cards.x:
The antibody screen looks for unexpected circulating immunoglobulin G alloantibodies against clinically significant red cell antigens, such as Kell, Duffy, Kidd and Rh C or E. It is an indirect antiglobulin test.

The patient's plasma is incubated in vitro with 2 to 3 vials of group O reagent red cells that carry a comprehensive set of antigens. Antihuman globulin is then added to crosslink any immunoglobulin G-coated cells, producing visible agglutination.

- Negative screen: no unexpected red cell antibodies, about 95 to 98% of patients.
- Positive screen: the patient has formed an alloantibody from a prior transfusion, transplantation or pregnancy.

cards.t: Antibody identification and high-risk specificities
q: what happens after a positive antibody screen
why does a positive screen delay blood
which antibodies are high risk
cards.x:
When the screen is positive, an 11- to 16-cell panel is tested to map the antibody's specificity, meaning exactly which antigen it targets.

The high-risk specificities are anti-Kell (anti-K), anti-Kidd (anti-Jka and anti-Jkb), anti-Duffy (anti-Fya) and anti-Rh (anti-c and anti-E).

Once the antibody is known, the blood bank must phenotypically screen donor units to find red cells that lack that antigen, then crossmatch them. This can take hours or days, so the type and screen should be ordered well in advance of elective procedures.

cards.t: Crossmatching: electronic, immediate spin and full antiglobulin
q: what are the types of crossmatch
when is an electronic crossmatch used
why does a positive antibody screen make crossmatching slower
cards.x:
The crossmatch checks that a donor unit is compatible with this recipient, and how much work it takes depends on the screen and antibody history.

- Electronic: needs a negative antibody screen and at least two concordant blood type records on file. Validated software checks ABO (blood group system) and Rh compatibility, with no technician pipetting, in under a minute.
- Immediate spin: negative screen and no history of clinically significant alloantibodies. Recipient serum is mixed with donor red cells at room temperature and centrifuged, as a final check for ABO compatibility and clerical mismatch, in about 5 to 10 minutes.
- Antiglobulin crossmatch: positive screen or documented history of clinically significant antibodies. Incubation at 37 degrees C, then antihuman globulin (Coombs serum) detects weak immunoglobulin G binding to minor red cell antigens. It takes 45 to 60 or more minutes per unit.

cards.t: Direct antiglobulin test (direct Coombs)
q: what does the direct antiglobulin test show
when is a direct antiglobulin test ordered
what does a positive direct antiglobulin test mean
cards.x:
The direct antiglobulin test asks: are the patient's red blood cells already coated with antibodies or complement inside the body?

It uses the patient's own washed circulating red cells, so any attachment happened in vivo. The reagent is polyspecific antihuman globulin (anti-immunoglobulin G plus anti-C3d). If it is positive, the cells are tested with monospecific anti-immunoglobulin G and anti-C3d.

Agglutination is positive and confirms immune-mediated red cell coating. It is used in the workup of acute or delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions, autoimmune hemolytic anemia and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

cards.t: Indirect antiglobulin test (indirect Coombs)
q: what does the indirect antiglobulin test show
what is the difference between direct and indirect Coombs
when is an indirect antiglobulin test used
cards.x:
The indirect antiglobulin test asks: does the patient have free, unbound antibodies in the plasma that could attack donor cells?

The patient's plasma or serum is incubated in vitro with known reagent red cells, then antihuman globulin is added after incubation and washing. Agglutination is positive and proves a circulating alloantibody.

It is used for pre-transfusion antibody screening, maternal prenatal antibody screens and compatibility crossmatching.

Quick contrast: the direct test uses the patient's own cells to see what is already stuck on them. The indirect test uses the patient's plasma to see what free antibody it holds.

cards.t: Type and screen compared with type and crossmatch
q: what is the difference between type and screen and type and crossmatch
when do you order a type and screen
why does a type and crossmatch reserve units
cards.x:
These two orders sit at different steps of the testing sequence.

- Type and screen: determines ABO (blood group system) and Rh and tests plasma for unexpected alloantibodies. No units are assigned or held. It fits when a transfusion is possible but not immediately expected, such as routine surgery or a stable gastrointestinal bleed. It preserves inventory, and if blood is needed, units can be crossmatched rapidly.
- Type and crossmatch: completes the type and screen and physically matches donor units to the patient's serum. Specific numbered units are tagged and reserved. It fits when transfusion is planned, highly probable or actively ongoing.

Held units are unavailable to other patients until explicitly released. A positive screen requires an antibody panel and a full antihuman globulin crossmatch.

cards.t: The 3-day specimen rule
q: when does a type and screen sample expire
why is the sample valid for only 3 days
who needs a new blood sample every 3 days
cards.x:
A type and screen sample is valid for only 72 hours (3 days) if the patient meets any of three conditions: transfused within the prior 3 months, pregnant within the prior 3 months, or has an uncertain clinical history.

The rationale is that new alloantibodies can form rapidly after a secondary exposure, so an old sample might miss an antibody that has appeared since.

If the sample expires, the patient needs a full redraw and repeat testing.

cards.t: What to do first for any suspected transfusion reaction
q: what do you do first if you suspect a transfusion reaction
should you slow the transfusion or stop it
what do you do with the blood bag after a reaction
cards.x:
For any suspected reaction, the first steps are the same, whatever type it turns out to be.

1. Stop the infusion immediately. Do not slow it; halt it and disconnect the tubing from the intravenous catheter hub.
2. Keep intravenous access open with fresh normal saline and new tubing. Never flush the remaining blood in the line into the patient.
3. Do a clerical recheck at the bedside: compare the wristband against the unit label, the bag paperwork and the compatibility slip.
4. Notify the blood bank and the attending.
5. Return the bag, intact tubing and attached tags to the blood bank.
6. Draw post-reaction labs.

cards.t: Post-reaction workup: what the blood bank and labs check
q: what labs are drawn after a suspected transfusion reaction
why send the blood bag back
what does the blood bank do after a reaction
cards.x:
After the transfusion is stopped, the blood bank and the lab work to find out what happened.

The blood bank inspects post-transfusion samples and verifies donor lots. The remaining product, the intact tubing and all attached tags go back to the blood bank for testing and cultures.

Fresh blood and urine are drawn for: repeat ABO (blood group system) and Rh typing, direct antiglobulin test, complete blood count, metabolic panel, free plasma hemoglobin and urinalysis. Together these look for red cell destruction and recheck the blood type.

cards.t: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
q: what is an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
what are the signs of an acute hemolytic reaction
how fast does an acute hemolytic reaction start
cards.x:
An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is intravascular collapse caused by ABO (blood group system) incompatibility, in over 90% of cases a clerical error. Immunoglobulin M and complement lyse the donor red cells inside the bloodstream.

It starts within minutes of beginning the transfusion, and as little as 25 mL can be fatal.

The classic triad is high fever and rigors, flank or lower back pain (from renal vasoconstriction), and red or dark urine (hemoglobinuria, free hemoglobin in the urine).

Severe cases add a sense of impending doom, dyspnea, hypotension and shock, acute tubular necrosis, and catastrophic disseminated intravascular coagulation with bleeding from intravenous sites.

cards.t: Lab findings in an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
q: what labs show an acute hemolytic reaction
can the direct antiglobulin test be negative in an acute hemolytic reaction
what happens to haptoglobin and lactate dehydrogenase in an acute hemolytic reaction
cards.x:
The labs show red cells breaking apart, along with clotting abnormalities.

- Direct antiglobulin test: newly positive, because anti-A or anti-B coats the remaining cells. It may be negative if all the donor cells are instantly lysed.
- Plasma and urine: pink or red plasma (hemoglobinemia) and red urine (hemoglobinuria).
- Hemolysis profile: undetectable haptoglobin, markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, then a rise in indirect bilirubin.
- Coagulation (disseminated intravascular coagulation): prolonged prothrombin time and international normalized ratio (INR) and partial thromboplastin time, high D-dimer, low fibrinogen and platelets.
- Renal: rising urea nitrogen and creatinine, and hyperkalemia.

cards.t: Managing an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
q: how is an acute hemolytic reaction managed
why give aggressive fluids in a hemolytic reaction
what organs are at risk in an acute hemolytic reaction
cards.x:
After the universal first steps (stop the blood, keep saline running, recheck, notify the blood bank), management focuses on the shock and on protecting the kidneys.

- Aggressive intravenous hydration, with a target urine output of 100 to 200 mL per hour, and maintaining renal perfusion. This protects the kidneys, which are at risk because free hemoglobin damages the tubules.
- Vasopressors for shock.

The feared complications are acute tubular necrosis from the free hemoglobin and disseminated intravascular coagulation, with bleeding from intravenous sites.

cards.t: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction
q: what is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction
what is the anamnestic trap
when does a delayed hemolytic reaction happen
cards.x:
A delayed hemolytic reaction is a secondary (anamnestic, or memory) immunoglobulin G response against minor red cell antigens such as Kidd, Rh, Duffy and Kell. It appears typically 3 to 30 days after transfusion, peaking at 5 to 15 days.

The anamnestic trap: the patient's historical antibody was undetectable on the pre-transfusion screen. Re-exposure to the donor antigen restarts rapid immunoglobulin G production.

It is often indolent or silent: an unexplained drop in hemoglobin (or failure to rise by 1 g/dL per unit), low-grade fever and mild jaundice.

Clearance is extravascular, by splenic macrophages, so hemodynamic collapse is rare.

cards.t: Lab findings, sickle cell risk and hyperhemolysis in delayed reactions
q: what labs show a delayed hemolytic reaction
why is sickle cell disease a risk for delayed reactions
what is hyperhemolysis syndrome
cards.x:
The labs in a delayed hemolytic reaction point to extravascular destruction of the transfused cells.

- A newly positive direct antiglobulin test (immunoglobulin G coating the transfused cells).
- A newly positive antibody screen with a new alloantibody identified, for example anti-Jka.
- Elevated lactate dehydrogenase and indirect bilirubin, reduced haptoglobin, and spherocytes on the peripheral smear.

Sickle cell disease alert: these patients are at high risk of a delayed reaction that mimics a vaso-occlusive pain crisis, with hemoglobin A falling disproportionately.

Hyperhemolysis syndrome is when antibodies destroy both donor cells and the patient's own red cells. Reticulocytopenia develops, and further transfusions can be fatal.

cards.t: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction
q: what is a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction
what causes a fever during a transfusion
how common is a febrile transfusion reaction
cards.x:
A febrile non-hemolytic reaction is a fever caused by the blood product, not by red cell destruction. It is common, about 1% of transfusions, and higher with platelets.

The definition is a temperature rise of at least 1 degree C (1.8 degrees F) to at least 38 degrees C (100.4 degrees F) during or within 4 hours of transfusion, often with chills, rigors, headache and malaise.

There are two causes: cytokines (interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha) that build up in stored plasma, and recipient antibodies against donor white blood cell (human leukocyte antigen) antigens.

Blood pressure and breathing stay completely stable.

cards.t: Febrile reaction: a diagnosis of exclusion, sepsis check and treatment
q: how is a febrile non-hemolytic reaction diagnosed
when should I worry about sepsis with a transfusion fever
how is a febrile reaction prevented
cards.x:
A febrile non-hemolytic reaction is a diagnosis of exclusion. The laboratory workup is completely normal: direct antiglobulin test negative; free plasma and urine hemoglobin negative; haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase and bilirubin normal; and the blood bag Gram stain and culture negative.

Rule out sepsis: work up for bacterial sepsis if the fever is 2 degrees C or more, the patient is hypotensive, or the product was platelets.

Treatment is antipyretics (acetaminophen), with meperidine for severe shaking rigors. Pre-storage leukoreduction (removing white cells before storage) dramatically reduces rates. Routine premedication is discouraged.

cards.t: Allergic transfusion reaction
q: what is an allergic transfusion reaction
what are the signs of a mild allergic transfusion reaction
what causes an allergic transfusion reaction
cards.x:
An allergic transfusion reaction is a type I hypersensitivity. Preformed recipient immunoglobulin E reacts against soluble donor plasma proteins, causing localized mast cell activation.

It is common, 1 to 3% of transfusions, and most frequent with plasma-rich products such as fresh frozen plasma and platelets.

The presentation is pruritus (itching), localized urticaria (hives), erythema (redness) and flushing. The strict negative criteria matter: no fever or chills, no respiratory distress or wheezing, and no hypotension or tachycardia. Labs are normal, with a negative direct antiglobulin test and no hemolysis markers.

cards.t: The allergic reaction restart rule
q: can a transfusion be restarted after an allergic reaction
what is the restart rule
when should I not restart a transfusion
cards.x:
The allergic reaction is the only transfusion reaction in which the unit can be restarted.

1. Pause the infusion temporarily while evaluating.
2. Give an antihistamine (H1-blocker), such as diphenhydramine.
3. Re-evaluate at 20 to 30 minutes and verify there are no systemic or cardiopulmonary signs.
4. If symptoms are strictly confined to the skin and completely resolve, the same unit may be restarted at a slower rate within the 4-hour hang time limit.
5. Red flag: if fever, dyspnea, wheezing or hypotension occur, do not restart. Escalate to the full reaction protocol.

cards.t: Anaphylactic transfusion reaction and anti-IgA
q: what causes anaphylaxis during a transfusion
why does IgA deficiency matter in transfusion
how fast does transfusion anaphylaxis start
cards.x:
The classic cause of transfusion anaphylaxis is a patient with severe congenital immunoglobulin A deficiency (below 0.05 mg/dL) who has formed circulating anti-IgA antibodies. The trigger is donor plasma that contains normal immunoglobulin A.

It is sudden, within seconds to minutes after only 1 to 5 mL of product.

The presentation (with no fever) is laryngeal edema, stridor, bronchospasm and dyspnea; rapid circulatory collapse with severe hypotension and shock; and angioedema, generalized flushing, nausea and vomiting.

Key contrast: the absence of fever distinguishes anaphylaxis from septic shock and from acute hemolytic reactions.

cards.t: Managing transfusion anaphylaxis
q: what is the first-line treatment for transfusion anaphylaxis
should I give antihistamines or epinephrine first
what blood products can an anti-IgA patient get in the future
cards.x:
First-line treatment is intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh. Never delay epinephrine for antihistamines or steroids.

Supportive care is high-flow oxygen, airway protection and aggressive intravenous crystalloid boluses.

Diagnostic testing is a serum tryptase (drawn within 1 to 3 hours), a quantitative immunoglobulin A level and anti-IgA antibody titers.

For future transfusions, the patient needs washed red cells, which strip out plasma immunoglobulin A, or products from verified IgA-deficient donors.

cards.t: The five transfusion reactions side by side
k: acute vs delayed vs febrile vs allergic vs anaphylaxis
q: how do I tell the transfusion reactions apart
which transfusion reaction has fever and a negative direct antiglobulin test
what is the timing of each transfusion reaction
cards.x:
Timing, fever, shock and the direct antiglobulin test sort the five reactions.

- Acute hemolytic: minutes to 24 hours; fever yes; shock yes; direct antiglobulin test newly positive (though it may be negative if all donor cells are instantly lysed); marked hemolysis (pink plasma, red urine, low haptoglobin, high lactate dehydrogenase); clues are an ABO (blood group system) mismatch on recheck and acute disseminated intravascular coagulation.
- Delayed hemolytic: 3 to 30 days; fever mild or variable; shock rare; direct antiglobulin test newly positive; extravascular hemolysis; new alloantibody on the screen.
- Febrile non-hemolytic: during to 4 hours; fever yes; no shock; test negative; normal labs.
- Allergic: during to 4 hours; no fever; no shock; test negative; itching and hives that respond to an antihistamine.
- Anaphylaxis: seconds to minutes; no fever; shock yes; test negative; stridor, wheezing, high tryptase and anti-IgA.

cards.t: How the direct antiglobulin test separates hemolytic reactions
q: how do I tell a hemolytic from a non-hemolytic reaction
what does a newly positive direct antiglobulin test mean
why can the direct antiglobulin test be negative in acute hemolysis
cards.x:
The direct antiglobulin test detects antibodies bound to red cells in vivo. A newly positive result is the hallmark of immune hemolysis, so it separates the hemolytic reactions from the non-hemolytic ones.

- Newly positive: acute and delayed hemolytic reactions.
- Negative: febrile non-hemolytic, allergic and anaphylactic reactions.

The one catch is the acute hemolytic reaction, where the test may be negative if all the donor cells are instantly lysed, leaving nothing coated to detect.

cards.t: The universal emergency protocol for any suspected reaction (short version)
k: what to do for any transfusion reaction
q: what is the universal emergency protocol for a transfusion reaction
what do I do for any suspected transfusion reaction in short
when is epinephrine given in a transfusion reaction
cards.x:
Whatever kind of reaction you suspect, the same short list applies. Stop the blood, keep intravenous access open with saline, check vital signs, do the clerical check, and notify the blood bank.

The one extra step is for anaphylaxis: give intramuscular epinephrine. Because the first moves are identical for every reaction, you do not need to know which reaction it is before you act.
